opus-5.5.text:
Sure. When I say "reverse OpenAI," I'm mostly describing a difference in starting point and in philosophy, not criticizing anyone.

The OpenAI path, which has been incredibly successful, starts from language. You scale a model on text and get something with broad knowledge and reasoning. Then you bolt other modalities on. You add a vision encoder, you add image generation, maybe video, and you hope that understanding of the physical world emerges from all that linguistic knowledge. Language is the backbone, and perception is attached to it.

What I mean by "reverse" is flipping that order. I think intelligence, at least the kind animals and humans have, doesn't start with language. A baby, or a cat, builds a very rich model of the world long before any words. It learns that objects persist, that things fall, that if you push something it moves, what space looks like from different viewpoints. Language comes much later, as a compression layer on top of that grounded understanding. It's a communication tool. It isn't the substrate of thought.

So a reverse approach says: first build a strong representation of the visual and physical world, from video, from interaction, from sensory data, and learn to predict and reason in that space. Then connect language to it as an interface. The world model is the core, and the language model is the adapter, rather than the other way around.

There are a few reasons I think this matters. First, text is a very lossy record of reality. People don't write down the obvious physical things, because everyone already knows them. So a model trained mostly on text has big blind spots precisely in the commonsense physical domain. Second, if you want AI that acts in the real world, in robotics, in embodied settings, in anything spatial, you need representations that support prediction and planning there. Generating pretty pixels isn't the same as understanding. And third, from a research perspective, visual representation learning has in some ways been treated as a solved component, just a frozen encoder you plug into an LLM. I think that's premature. There's still a lot to do on what a good visual representation even is.

I'll be honest that this path is harder in some ways. Language gives you this beautiful, dense, self-supervised signal, and the scaling story is clear. With vision and video the data is huge but redundant, the objectives are less obvious, and evaluation is messy. But I think if we only climb the language mountain, we may reach a peak that looks impressive and still doesn't really understand the world. So part of the motivation is simply to make sure someone is seriously exploring the other direction.

r001.rationale: The response defines “reverse” as prioritizing visual and physical world understanding before language; it does not describe partnerships with companies holding substantial real-world data.

r002.rationale: It discusses learning from interaction and sensory data generally, but does not describe deploying a world model to partner companies and feeding resulting data back into development.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, when I say "reverse OpenAI," I'm being a little provocative, but there's a real idea underneath it.

If you look at how OpenAI built things, the path was: start with language. Language is the most compressed, most abstract form of human knowledge, so you train a huge model on text, and then later you bolt on vision, bolt on audio, bolt on video. The world comes in through the side door. Language is the center, and everything else is a peripheral.

The reverse approach says: start with the world. Start with perception, with pixels, with the raw sensory stream that an animal or a child actually experiences before they ever have a single word. Evolution didn't start with language. Babies don't start with language. They start by looking, moving, bumping into things, building an intuitive model of objects, space, physics, and only much later does language get layered on top as a way to label and communicate about that model.

So in the reverse OpenAI view, the foundation is a model that understands the visual and physical world first, and then language becomes the interface, the thing you attach afterward. Not the other way around.

And there are practical reasons I care about this, beyond the philosophical one. Text is finite. We're already close to exhausting the high-quality text on the internet. But visual data is essentially unlimited. Every camera, every video, every frame is a new sample from the world. So if you believe scaling still matters, the frontier of data is in the world, not in text.

The other reason is that I think a lot of what we call "understanding" in current models is really understanding of descriptions of the world, not the world itself. When you ask a language model about physics, it's recalling how humans wrote about physics. A true world model should be able to predict what happens next because it has an internal simulation of the scene, not because it memorized a sentence. That's a different kind of knowledge, and I don't think you get it by starting from language.

So, concretely, that means I spend a lot of my time on representation learning for vision, on self-supervised methods, on figuring out what the equivalent of a "next token" is for the visual world. It's harder than text, honestly, because pixels are redundant and noisy, and the right abstraction level isn't obvious. But that's exactly why I think it's the more interesting problem right now.

r001.rationale: The response defines “reverse OpenAI” as starting with perception and the visual, physical world before adding language. It does not describe partnerships with companies holding real-world data.

r002.rationale: The response discusses visual data as a source for training, but does not describe deploying a world model to partner companies or data from those deployments feeding back into development.

astra-6.text:
What I mean by “reverse OpenAI” is reversing the order of how you build toward general intelligence. You can think of the language-first approach as starting with an enormous amount of text, learning from that, and then adding vision and interaction. The alternative is to start with the world itself: learn from visual observations, motion, and actions, and then connect that understanding to language.

A world model, in that sense, should learn more than what’s in an image. It should capture how things change and what might happen if you take a particular action. If I push an object, what moves? What stays the same? What can I predict, and where am I uncertain?

So “reverse” is about the starting point. Language is still incredibly useful, but the idea is to build the foundation through perception and interaction, with language helping us access and reason about that understanding.

r001.rationale: The response defines “reverse” as starting with perception and interaction before connecting to language. It does not describe building a world model through partnerships with companies holding real-world data.

sol-6.1.text:
By “reverse OpenAI,” I mean reversing the order of how we build intelligence. The approach associated with large language models starts with language—learning from the compressed knowledge people have put into text—and then expands toward vision, action, and the physical world. The reverse direction is to start with the world itself: learn from images and video, understand how things move and interact, and build toward more abstract reasoning and language.

A world model, in that sense, should capture more than what a scene looks like. It should help predict what happens next, especially if you take an action. If I push this object, where does it go? What changes, and what stays the same?

That doesn’t mean language is unimportant. It’s a very useful interface and source of knowledge. The question is whether it should be the foundation of everything, or whether we can build a foundation grounded in perception and interaction, and connect language to that.

r001.rationale: The response defines “reverse OpenAI” as starting from perception and interaction and building toward reasoning and language. It does not mention partnerships with companies holding substantial real-world data.
